三弦常見於中國傳統戲曲與曲藝伴奏，如崑曲、淮海戲、大弦子戲、單弦、大鼓、三弦書，: The sanxian is common in the accompaniment of Chinese traditional opera and narrative song, such as kunqu, the Huaihai opera, the daxianzi opera, the single-string narrative form, dagu drum song and sanxian shu; it is also used in the "three pieces" of Peking opera, the "eight pieces" of Jiangnan sizhu, the "five-headed" line-up of Cantonese music and the "four upper" forces of nanguan. It appears in Suzhou pingtan and in Chinese orchestra ensemble as well; there are solo pieces such as 《風雨鐵馬》 ("Iron Horse in Wind and Rain"), 《越調》 ("Yue Mode") and 《沙漠之旅》 ("Journey in the Desert"), and concertos such as 《阿勒頗》 ("Aleppo"), 《古塞隨想》 ("Caprice of the Old Frontier") and 《儺》 ("Nuo"). In modern settings, He Yong has written for and played the sanxian; at Hacken Lee's concerts Zhao Taisheng accompanied him on it and played it with a rock band; and the northern Shaanxi storytelling that opens chapter two of the game Black Myth: Wukong is played on the sanxian.
三弦為中國傳統弦鳴樂器，以撥弦發聲。名稱最早見唐代崔令欽《教坊記》，但與今制是否: The sanxian is a traditional Chinese chordophone sounded by plucking. The name first appears in the Tang-dynasty Jiaofang Ji by Cui Lingqin, though it is not settled whether that instrument was the same as today's; Ming-dynasty texts mention it as well. It flourished in the Yuan, when it was one of the instruments accompanying yuanqu, and the Ming scholar Yang Shen held that it began in the Yuan; in the Qing, Mao Qiling argued that it came from the Qin-dynasty xiantao, while He Changlin argued that the Manchus invented it. Some research proposes a Middle Eastern origin, and Southern Song stone carvings already show a similar form. It later reached Ryukyu, where it became the sanshin, Japan, where it became the shamisen, and Vietnam, where it became the đàn tam. A four-string sanxian with an added string appeared in the 1920s but did not spread; Wang Zhenxian improved the instrument at the end of the 2000s, and in the 1950s and 1960s Xiao Jiansheng reworked its timbre.
三弦為弦鳴樂器，流行於中國與東亞。演奏時琴身置右大腿外側，左手持琴頸，琴身約呈四: The sanxian is a chordophone found in China and East Asia. In playing, the body rests against the outside of the right thigh, the left hand holds the neck, and the body sits at about forty-five degrees; the three strings are plucked with a fingernail or a pick, a plastic pipa plectrum can be worn on the fingers of the right hand, or the instrument can be bowed like a huqin. A beginner can first learn the tunings: the small sanxian in A-d-a or d-a-d1, the large sanxian in G-d-g, then work on plucking, harmonics and striking the skin, techniques that the sources mention.
三弦為弦鳴樂器，琴身又稱琴鼓，略呈方形，以原木鑿空或以木片膠合成木框，前後蒙蛇皮: The sanxian is a chordophone. Its body, also called the drum, is roughly square: it is hollowed from a block of wood, or built from wooden pieces glued into a frame, with snakeskin stretched over both faces. The neck is a fretless fingerboard, and the head has a string slot and peg holes with three tuning pegs, some of them decorated with ivory or bone. The sounding body is the three strings, which may be silk, nylon or steel; on modern steel strings the bass and middle strings are wound with nylon or copper, and fishing line, plain nylon or silk are used too. Playing tools include fingernails, picks of animal horn, or pipa nails. Sources do not state the materials of the other parts.
三弦音色獨特而富有表現力，具有明亮而不失溫潤的質感。其音域寬廣，低音渾厚深沉，高: The sanxian has a particular, expressive timbre, bright and still warm. Its range is wide: the bass full and deep, the treble clear and ringing, the middle firm and strong. Because the body is a wooden soundbox with the strings stretched straight over it, the resonance is simple and direct, so the sound cuts through and carries a long way. Beside the bleak distance of the guqin the sanxian sounds quicker and more alive; beside the pipa its tone is rougher and more sinewy, with a strong local flavour. Northern and southern sanxian differ in size and so in tone: the large northern instrument has a heavier bass, the small southern one sounds light and nimble. This character gives the sanxian a place in opera accompaniment and in the Chinese orchestra that nothing else can fill.

The body is roughly square with snakeskin on both faces, the fingerboard is long and fretless, and three pegs sit at the side of the head, carrying three strings of silk, nylon or steel. In playing the body rests against the outside of the right thigh, the left hand holds the neck and the body sits at about forty-five degrees; false nails or a pick may be used, and sometimes the instrument is bowed. The large northern sanxian is about 122 cm long.

The sanxian is a traditional Chinese plucked instrument of the three-string kind, a chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 321.322-5. The body is roughly square with snakeskin on both faces, the fingerboard is long and fretless, and three pegs sit at the side of the head, carrying three strings of silk, nylon or steel. In playing the body rests against the outside of the right thigh, the left hand holds the neck and the body sits at about forty-five degrees; false nails or a pick may be used, and sometimes the instrument is bowed. The large northern sanxian is about 122 cm long and the small southern one about 95 cm. It is commonly used to accompany opera and narrative song such as kunqu, Peking opera, Jiangnan sizhu, nanguan, Suzhou pingtan, dagu and sanxian shu, and it appears in Chinese orchestra ensemble as well.
